questions.question: Which national initiative aims to prevent and control non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension?

options.text: National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS)**, which has been recently renamed as the **National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD)**, was launched in **2010**. It is the primary initiative in **India** dedicated to managing chronic lifestyle diseases.

• The program focuses on **health promotion**, **early diagnosis**, and **management** of **NCDs**. It aims to strengthen **infrastructure**, develop **human resources**, and provide **palliative care**. This is the correct option as it directly targets **diabetes** and **hypertension**.

• **Mission Indradhanush** is a health mission launched in **December 2014**. Its goal is to ensure full **immunization** coverage for children up to **2 years** of age and **pregnant women** against **12 vaccine-preventable diseases**. It does not focus on **NCDs** like **diabetes**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

• The **National Digital Health Mission (NDHM)**, now known as the **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM)**, was launched in **August 2020**. It focuses on creating a **digital health ecosystem** including **Health IDs** and **Electronic Health Records**. It is a technological framework, not a clinical control program for **NCDs**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

• **Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY)** is the **insurance** component of **Ayushman Bharat**, providing a cover of **Rs. 5 lakh** per family per year for **secondary** and **tertiary care** hospitalization. While it covers treatment for **NCDs**, it is not a dedicated preventive and control initiative like **NP-NCD**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs)**: These are medical conditions that are not infectious and cannot be passed from person to person. In **India**, **NCDs** are responsible for nearly **63%** of all deaths. The four major types are **cardiovascular diseases**, **cancers**, **chronic respiratory diseases**, and **diabetes**.

• **75/25 Initiative**: Launched by the **Union Health Ministry**, this initiative aims to ensure that **75 million** people suffering from **hypertension** and **diabetes** are put on standard care by the year **2025** through **Primary Health Centres**.

• **Ayushman Bharat - Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs)**: These centers are the frontline for **NCD** screening. Population-based screening for **hypertension**, **diabetes**, and common cancers (**oral**, **breast**, and **cervical**) is conducted for all individuals above the age of **30 years**.

• **Risk Factors**: The **NP-NCD** program specifically targets four major behavioral risk factors: **tobacco use**, **unhealthy diet**, **physical inactivity**, and **harmful use of alcohol**.

• **Global Targets**: **India** was the first country to adopt the **Global Monitoring Framework** for **NCDs**, aiming for a **25%** relative reduction in premature mortality from **NCDs** by **2025**, as aligned with the **Sustainable Development Goals (SDG)** target **3.4**.

**Important Points__**

• **India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI)**: This is a **multi-partner** initiative involving the **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare**, **ICMR**, and **WHO**. It won the **2022 UN Interagency Task Force** award for its excellence in scaling up **hypertension** control within the primary health care system.

• **National Health Policy (NHP) 2017**: This policy emphasizes the need for **preventive** and **promotive** health care. It set a target to reduce the prevalence of **tobacco use** by **15%** by **2020** and **30%** by **2025** to combat **NCDs**.

• **Portal for NCDs**: The government has developed a **National NCD Portal** to facilitate the **real-time monitoring** of screening and treatment data across the country, ensuring better follow-up for patients with **chronic conditions**.

• **Financial Support**: Under the **National Health Mission (NHM)**, states receive financial and technical support for setting up **NCD Clinics** at the **District** and **Community Health Centre (CHC)** levels.
</ul

questions.question: If the length of a wire is doubled and its thickness (cross-sectional area) is reduced to half, what will be the effect on its electrical resistance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It becomes four times**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **electrical resistance** (R) of a conductor is directly proportional to its **length** (L) and inversely proportional to its **cross-sectional area** (A). This relationship is expressed by the formula: R = rho (L)/(A) , where rho (rho) is the **resistivity** of the material.

• According to the question, the new length (L') is twice the original length (L' = 2L) and the new cross-sectional area (A') is half of the original area (A' = A/2).

• Substituting these new values into the resistance formula: Rₙₑw = rho (2L)/(A/2) .

• By simplifying the expression, we get: Rₙₑw = rho (2L times 2)/(A) = 4 times (rho (L)/(A)) .

• Therefore, the new resistance is **four times** the original resistance (R_new = 4R).

• **Option 1, 2, and 4** are incorrect because they do not satisfy the mathematical relationship derived from the doubling of length and halving of the area simultaneously.

**Additional Information__**

• **Resistivity** ( rho ) is an intrinsic property of a material and does not change with the dimensions (length or area) of the wire; it only changes with **temperature** and the **nature of the material**.

• The **SI unit** of electrical resistance is the **Ohm** (Ω).

• **Ohm's Law** states that the current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points, provided temperature remains constant (V = IR).

• Factors affecting the resistance of a wire include:
 
 
• **Length**: Longer wires have more resistance.
 
• **Thickness (Area)**: Thicker wires have less resistance.
 
• **Temperature**: For most metals, resistance increases as temperature increases.
 
• **Material**: Different materials (like copper vs. nichrome) have different resistivities.

questions.question:
Fill in the blank:
The sex ratio in India refers to the number of females per ____ males.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1000**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **sex ratio** is a critical demographic indicator used to describe the number of **females** per **1000 males** in a given population. It is used to measure the extent of prevailing equity between males and females in a society at a given point in time.

• In **India**, the sex ratio is calculated as the number of females divided by the number of males, multiplied by **1000**. This standard is followed by the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India** during the decadal **Census** operations.

• The options **1200**, **990**, and **1050** are incorrect because they do not represent the official base unit for demographic measurement in the **Indian** context. The denominator for calculating the sex ratio is universally fixed at **1000 males** in official reports.

• This metric is essential for understanding the **gender balance**, **socio-economic status**, and **health** of the female population. A skewed sex ratio often indicates deep-rooted social issues like **gender discrimination** and **female foeticide**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• According to the **Census 2011**, the national sex ratio of **India** was **943** females per **1000 males**, which showed a slight improvement from the **2001 Census** figure of **933**.

• The **Child Sex Ratio**, defined for the age group **0-6 years**, was recorded at **919** in the **2011 Census**, which was a decline from **927** in **2001**, raising significant concerns about the survival of the girl child.

• Among the states, **Kerala** holds the distinction of having the highest sex ratio in **India** with **1084** females per **1000 males** as per the **2011 Census**. Conversely, **Haryana** recorded the lowest among states at **879**.

• Among Union Territories, **Puducherry** has the highest sex ratio at **1037**, while **Daman and Diu** recorded the lowest at **618** in the **2011** data.

• The **National Family Health Survey-5 (NFHS-5)**, conducted between **2019-21**, reported a sex ratio of **1020** females per **1000 males**, indicating a demographic shift, though this data is survey-based and not a complete enumeration like the **Census**.

**Important Points__**

• The **Government of India** launched the **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (BBBP)** scheme on **22 January 2015** at **Panipat, Haryana**, to address the declining child sex ratio and promote women's empowerment through education.

• The **Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994**, was enacted to stop female foeticide and arrest the declining sex ratio by prohibiting **sex determination** before or after conception.

• Factors influencing the sex ratio include **maternal mortality**, **sex-selective abortion**, **literacy rates**, and **differential life expectancy** between genders.

• The **Son Meta-Preference**, a term used in the **Economic Survey 2017-18**, describes the societal desire for a male child, which significantly impacts the sex ratio in several Indian states.
</ul

questions.question: In India, which of the following statement is correct about the financial relation between the Center and the States?

options.text: The Union Government has exclusive control over all types of taxation, including state taxes.
The States have no role in the allocation of taxes and resources, and all funds are directly managed by the Union.
The Union Government collects taxes and distributes them between the Union and the States through the Finance Commission.
States have the authority to impose taxes on defense, currency, and foreign trade.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Union Government collects taxes and distributes them between the Union and the States through the Finance Commission**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The financial relations between the **Union** and the **States** are primarily governed by **Articles 264 to 293** in **Part XII** of the **Constitution of India**. The **Constitution** provides for a clear division of taxing powers between the two levels of government to ensure fiscal federalism.

• Statement 1: The **Union Government** has exclusive control over all types of taxation, including state taxes. This is incorrect because the **Seventh Schedule** of the **Constitution** divides the power to levy taxes into three lists: the **Union List**, the **State List**, and the **Concurrent List**. **States** have the exclusive power to tax items like **land revenue**, **agricultural income**, and **state excise duties** on alcoholic liquors. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• Statement 2: The **States** have no role in the allocation of taxes and resources, and all funds are directly managed by the **Union**. This is incorrect because **States** manage their own **Consolidated Fund of the State** and play a vital role in the **GST Council** and the **Finance Commission** deliberations to determine resource sharing. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• Statement 3: The **Union Government** collects taxes and distributes them between the **Union** and the **States** through the **Finance Commission**. This is correct as **Article 280** mandates the **President of India** to constitute a **Finance Commission** every **five years** to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the **Center** and the **States**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***

• Statement 4: **States** have the authority to impose taxes on **defense**, **currency**, and **foreign trade**. This is incorrect because these subjects are part of the **Union List (List I)**, and only the **Parliament of India** has the authority to legislate and levy taxes on these national importance matters. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Finance Commission**: It is a **constitutional body** established under **Article 280**. The **15th Finance Commission**, chaired by **N.K. Singh**, recommended a **41%** share of the divisible pool of central taxes for **States** for the period **2021-2026**. The **16th Finance Commission** was recently constituted under the chairmanship of **Dr. Arvind Panagariya** in **December 2023**.

• **Goods and Services Tax (GST)**: Introduced by the **101st Amendment Act, 2016**, **GST** is a comprehensive indirect tax that replaced multiple central and state taxes. The **GST Council**, established under **Article 279A**, is a joint forum of the **Center** and the **States** that makes recommendations on tax rates, exemptions, and thresholds.

• **Grants-in-Aid**: Apart from tax sharing, the **Center** provides grants to **States**. **Statutory Grants** are given under **Article 275** based on the **Finance Commission’s** recommendations, while **Discretionary Grants** are provided under **Article 282** for public purposes or specific schemes.

• **Borrowing Powers**: Under **Article 292**, the **Union Government** can borrow upon the security of the **Consolidated Fund of India**. Under **Article 293**, **States** can borrow within **India** upon the security of the **Consolidated Fund of the State**, but they require the **Center’s** consent if they have any outstanding central loans.

**Important Points__**

• **Sarkaria Commission (1983)**: This commission was set up to review the **Center-State relations** and recommended that the **residuary powers** of taxation should remain with the **Parliament**, while other residuary powers should be moved to the **Concurrent List**.

• **Vertical vs Horizontal Devolution**: **Vertical Devolution** refers to the transfer of resources from the **Union** to the **States**. **Horizontal Devolution** is the formula used to distribute the **States’** share among individual **States** based on factors like **population (2011 census)**, **area**, **forest cover**, **income distance**, and **demographic performance**.

• **Article 265**: It ensures that **no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law**, protecting citizens from arbitrary taxation by either the **Central** or **State** governments.

• **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)**: Under **Article 148**, the **CAG** audits the accounts of both the **Union** and the **States**, ensuring financial accountability in the federal structure.

questions.question: Who wrote the book "Mein Kampf"?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Adolf Hitler**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Mein Kampf**, which translates to **'My Struggle'**, is an autobiographical manifesto written by the **Nazi Party** leader **Adolf Hitler**. It outlines his political ideology and future plans for **Germany**.

• The book was written while **Hitler** was imprisoned in **Landsberg Prison** in **1924**. He was serving a sentence for **high treason** following the failed **Beer Hall Putsch** (also known as the **Munich Putsch**) of **November 1923**.

• The work was published in two volumes: the first in **1925** and the second in **1926**. It was edited by **Hitler's** deputy, **Rudolf Hess**, who also took dictation for parts of the book while they were both in prison. ***Hence, Option 1 is correct.***

• The book was originally titled 'Four and a Half Years of Struggle against Lies, Stupidity and Cowardice', but the title was shortened to **Mein Kampf** by his publisher, **Max Amann**.

• In the book, **Hitler** details his childhood, his years in **Vienna**, and his experiences during **World War I**, while articulating his **anti-Semitic** and **nationalist** views.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Joseph Goebbels** (Option 2): He served as the **Reich Minister of Propaganda** of **Nazi Germany** from **1933 to 1945**. He was one of **Adolf Hitler's** closest and most devoted acolytes, known for his skills in public speaking and his deep-seated **anti-Semitism**.

• **Heinrich Himmler** (Option 3): He was the **Reichsführer of the Schutzstaffel (SS)** and a leading member of the **Nazi Party**. **Himmler** was one of the most powerful men in **Nazi Germany** and a main architect of the **Holocaust**.

• **Rudolf Hess** (Option 4): He was a prominent politician in **Nazi Germany** and served as **Deputy Führer** to **Adolf Hitler** from **1933 to 1941**. While he assisted in the creation of **Mein Kampf**, he is not the primary author.

• **Ideological Themes**: The book promotes the concept of **Lebensraum** (living space), asserting that **Germany** needed to expand its territory to the east, particularly into **Russia**, to sustain the **Aryan race**.

• **Impact**: After **Hitler** became **Chancellor of Germany** in **1933**, the book became a massive bestseller. It was considered the **'Bible of National Socialism'** and was frequently given as a gift to newlywed couples and soldiers.

**Important Points__**

• **Copyright History**: After **World War II** and **Hitler's** death in **1945**, the copyright of **Mein Kampf** was transferred to the state of **Bavaria**. The **Bavarian government** refused to allow any new editions to be printed in **Germany** to prevent the spread of **Nazi** ideology.

• **Public Domain**: The copyright expired on **December 31, 2015**, exactly **70 years** after the author's death. This led to the publication of a heavily **annotated edition** by the **Institute of Contemporary History** in **Munich** in **2016**, intended for academic and historical study.

• **Social Darwinism**: The book is heavily influenced by **Social Darwinism**, portraying human history as a perpetual struggle between races, with the **Aryan race** at the top of the hierarchy.

• **Global Reach**: Despite its controversial nature, the book has been translated into numerous languages and remains a subject of intense historical analysis to understand the roots of the **Third Reich** and the **Second World War**.

questions.question: The Bodhisattva statues of Gandhara show the influence of which artistic style?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Greek**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bodhisattva** statues of the **Gandhara School of Art** are a prime example of **Graeco-Buddhist art**, which combined **Indian** religious themes with **Greek** and **Roman** artistic techniques.

• The **Greek** influence is clearly visible in the **physiognomy** of the statues, featuring **wavy hair**, **sharp facial features**, **muscular bodies**, and **realistic anatomy**, which were inspired by **Hellenistic** sculptures of gods like **Apollo**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Greek.***

• The **drapery** or clothing depicted on these **Bodhisattva** figures resembles the **Roman toga**, characterized by **heavy, thick folds** and a realistic flow that follows the contours of the body.

• The **Gandhara** artists used **anthropomorphic** representations, depicting the **Buddha** and **Bodhisattvas** in human form with **idealized beauty**, a concept central to **Greek** art.

• Other options like **Mughal**, **Persian**, and **Rajput** are incorrect because they belong to different **chronological periods** or **cultural contexts**; for example, **Mughal** and **Rajput** styles emerged in the **medieval period**, long after the peak of **Gandhara** art.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Geographical Location and Period:** The **Gandhara School** flourished in the **northwestern** part of the **Indian subcontinent** (modern-day **Pakistan** and **Afghanistan**) from the **1st century BCE** to the **4th century CE**.

• **Patronage:** This artistic style received significant support from the **Kushan Empire**, particularly under the reign of **King Kanishka**, who was a great promoter of **Mahayana Buddhism**.

• **Materials Used:** Early **Gandhara** sculptures were primarily made of **grey schist** (a type of stone), while later works frequently utilized **stucco** (plaster) for finer detailing.

• **Depiction of Bodhisattvas:** Unlike the **Buddha**, who was often shown in simple robes, **Bodhisattvas** like **Maitreya** and **Avalokiteshvara** were depicted as **princes** wearing elaborate **jewelry**, **turbans**, **sandals**, and sometimes even **mustaches**.

• **Comparison with Mathura School:** While **Gandhara** art was **hybrid** and **realistic**, the **Mathura School** was **indigenous** and focused more on **symbolism** and **spiritual** expression using **spotted red sandstone**.

**Important Points__**

• **Cultural Syncretism:** The **Greek** influence reached the region following the conquests of **Alexander the Great** in **326 BCE** and the subsequent establishment of **Indo-Greek** kingdoms.

• **Artistic Features:** Key **Hellenistic** features include the **halo** (prabhamandala) which was initially plain in **Gandhara**, the **ushnisha** (cranial bump) styled like a **Greek topknot**, and the **meditative** yet **human-like** facial expressions.

• **Major Centers:** The prominent centers of **Gandhara** art were **Taxila**, **Peshawar** (Purushapura), **Bagram**, and **Bamiyan**.

• **Legacy:** This school played a crucial role in the spread of **Buddhist imagery** along the **Silk Road** to **Central Asia**, **China**, and **Japan**.
</ul

questions.question: Where is the BRICS headquarters located?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Shanghai**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The headquarters of the **New Development Bank (NDB)**, which is the primary financial and administrative institution of the **BRICS** nations, is located in **Shanghai**, **China**. While **BRICS** itself is an informal intergovernmental organization without a permanent secretariat, the **NDB** serves as its central physical hub.

• The **New Development Bank** was established following an agreement signed during the **6th BRICS Summit** held in **Fortaleza**, **Brazil**, in **July 2014**. It officially began its operations in **2015** to support infrastructure and sustainable development projects.

• The **Shanghai** headquarters is situated in the **Pudong Financial District**. The permanent headquarters building was officially inaugurated and handed over to the bank in **September 2021**.

• The first President of the **NDB** was **K.V. Kamath** from **India**, who served from **2015** to **2020**. Currently, the bank is headed by **Dilma Rousseff**, the former President of **Brazil**, who took office in **2023**.

• The other options—**Moscow** (Russia), **New Delhi** (India), and **Brasilia** (Brazil)—are the capital cities of member nations that host annual summits on a rotational basis but do not house the permanent headquarters of the **NDB**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Evolution of BRICS**: The acronym **BRIC** was originally coined by economist **Jim O’Neill** of **Goldman Sachs** in **2001** to highlight the economic potential of **Brazil**, **Russia**, **India**, and **China**. The group held its first formal summit in **Yekaterinburg**, **Russia**, in **2009**.

• **Inclusion of South Africa**: **South Africa** was invited to join the group in **December 2010**, and the acronym was updated to **BRICS**. The country attended its first summit in **Sanya**, **China**, in **2011**.

• **BRICS Expansion (2024)**: During the **15th BRICS Summit** in **Johannesburg**, **South Africa** (**2023**), the bloc announced a major expansion. As of **January 1, 2024**, **Egypt**, **Ethiopia**, **Iran**, and the **United Arab Emirates (UAE)** officially became members of the group.

• **Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA)**: Established alongside the **NDB** in **2015**, the **CRA** is a framework intended to provide liquidity support to member countries facing short-term balance of payments pressures, acting as a safety net similar to the **IMF**.

• **Economic Weight**: The expanded **BRICS** bloc represents approximately **45%** of the world’s population and nearly **28%** of the global **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** in nominal terms, significantly influencing global trade and energy markets.

**Important Points__**

• **Voting Power in NDB**: Unlike the **World Bank** or **IMF**, where voting power is tied to capital contribution, the **NDB** operates on a **one-country, one-vote** principle, ensuring that no single member has **veto power**.

• **Regional Offices**: To expand its reach, the **NDB** has established regional offices, including the **Africa Regional Center** in **Johannesburg**, the **Americas Regional Office** in **Sao Paulo**, and the **Indian Regional Office** at **GIFT City** in **Gujarat**.

• **Annual Presidency**: The chairship of **BRICS** rotates annually among the member nations. For the year **2024**, **Russia** held the **BRICS Presidency**, hosting the summit in **Kazan**.

questions.question: Where will India's Aditya-L1 mission be placed?

options.text: At the Sun-Earth L1 point in a halo orbit

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**At the Sun-Earth L1 point in a halo orbit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Aditya-L1** mission is **India’s first dedicated space mission** to study the **Sun**. It is designed to be placed in a **halo orbit** around the **Lagrangian point 1 (L1)** of the **Sun-Earth system**.
 
• The **Sun-Earth L1 point** is located approximately **1.5 million kilometers** away from the **Earth**, which is about **1%** of the total distance between the **Earth** and the **Sun**.
 
• A satellite placed in the **halo orbit** around the **L1 point** has the major advantage of continuously viewing the **Sun** without any **occultation** or **eclipses**. This allows for uninterrupted monitoring of **solar activities** and their impact on **space weather**.
 
• The **Lagrange points** are positions in space where the **gravitational forces** of a **two-body system** (like the Sun and Earth) produce enhanced regions of attraction and repulsion. These can be used by spacecraft to reduce **fuel consumption** needed to remain in position.
 
• Option 1 is incorrect because the **Sun-Earth L2 point** is located on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun and is typically used for **space telescopes** like the **James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)** to observe the deep universe.
 
• Option 3 is incorrect because the **Earth-Moon L1 point** is located between the Earth and the Moon, which is not suitable for a mission dedicated to **solar observation**.
 
• Option 4 is incorrect because the **Mars-Sun L1 point** would be located near **Mars**, which is far beyond the scope of a mission intended to monitor the Sun from the vicinity of **Earth**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Launch Details:** The **Aditya-L1** spacecraft was successfully launched on **September 2, 2023**, by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** using the **PSLV-C57** launch vehicle from the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre** in **Sriharikota**.
 
• **Mission Payloads:** The spacecraft carries **seven scientific payloads**. These include the **Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC)**, **Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT)**, **Solar Low Energy X-ray Spectrometer (SoLEXS)**, **High Energy L1 Orbiting X-ray Spectrometer (HEL1OS)**, **Aditya Solar wind Particle Experiment (ASPEX)**, **Plasma Analyser Package For Aditya (PAPA)**, and **Advanced Tri-axial High Resolution Digital Magnetometers**.
 
• **Scientific Objectives:** The mission aims to study the **solar corona** (the outermost layer), **photosphere**, and **chromosphere**. It also investigates **Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs)**, **solar flares**, and the **solar wind** to understand the dynamics of the **solar atmosphere** and **coronal heating**.
 
• **Mission Duration:** The mission has a planned life of approximately **5.2 years**, during which it will provide crucial data to predict **space weather** events that can affect **satellite communications** and **power grids** on Earth.
 
• **Lagrange Points:** There are five such points in the **Sun-Earth system**, labeled **L1 to L5**. **L1**, **L2**, and **L3** are unstable, while **L4** and **L5** are stable points.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Halo Orbit:** Unlike a simple circular orbit, a **halo orbit** is a three-dimensional, periodic orbit near the **L1 point**. It allows the spacecraft to stay out of the **Earth's shadow** and maintain a constant line of sight with both the **Sun** and **Earth** ground stations.
 
• **Distance Comparison:** The distance to **L1** (**1.5 million km**) is much greater than the distance to the **International Space Station (ISS)**, which orbits at about **400 km**, but it is much less than the distance to the **Sun** (about **150 million km**).
 
• **Global Context:** With the success of **Aditya-L1**, **India** joins a select group of nations and agencies, such as **NASA** and the **ESA**, that have placed observatories at the **L1 point** for solar research, following missions like **SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory)**.

questions.question: What has been observed in the past decade regarding earthquakes and subsurface fluids?

options.text: A decrease in earthquakes triggered by injection and production
No change in earthquakes triggered by injection and production
A substantial increase in earthquakes triggered by injection and production
Earthquakes are no longer triggered by injection and production

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A substantial increase in earthquakes triggered by injection and production**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• Over the past decade, scientific observations have confirmed a **substantial increase** in the frequency of earthquakes caused by human activities, a phenomenon known as **induced seismicity**.

• The primary cause of this increase is the **injection of fluids** into the subsurface, particularly the disposal of **wastewater** produced during oil and gas operations.

• When fluids are injected into deep disposal wells, they increase the **pore pressure** within the rock formations. This pressure can counteract the **frictional forces** holding a fault together, causing it to slip and trigger an earthquake.

• Regions that were historically seismically quiet, such as **Oklahoma**, **Texas**, and **Kansas** in the **United States**, have seen a dramatic rise in earthquake activity directly correlated with the expansion of **unconventional oil and gas production**.

• While **hydraulic fracturing** (fracking) itself can cause small tremors, the vast majority of significant induced earthquakes are linked to the long-term, high-volume **injection of waste fluids**.

**Additional Information__**

• The **United States Geological Survey (USGS)** now includes **induced earthquakes** in its short-term seismic hazard forecasts due to their increased frequency and potential for damage.

• In **Oklahoma**, the number of earthquakes with a magnitude of 3.0 or greater jumped from an average of **1.5 per year** prior to 2008 to a peak of **903 in 2015**.

• Mitigation strategies involve **seismic monitoring**, limiting **injection rates**, and avoiding injection near known **basement faults**.

• Apart from oil and gas, other activities like **geothermal energy production** and **carbon capture and storage (CCS)** also involve subsurface fluid management that requires careful monitoring to prevent **triggered seismicity**.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is a key feature of Mathura school of sculpture?

options.text: Iconography of Buddha and Hindu deities

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iconography of Buddha and Hindu deities**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Mathura school of sculpture** flourished primarily during the **Kushana period** between the **1st century AD** and the **3rd century AD**. It is celebrated for being an **indigenous style** of art that developed without significant foreign influence.

• A primary feature of this school is the **Iconography of Buddha and Hindu deities**. It was one of the earliest schools to create **anthropomorphic** (human) representations of the **Buddha**, alongside **Jain Tirthankaras** and **Hindu gods** like **Vishnu**, **Shiva**, **Surya**, and **Kubera**. ***Hence, the correct answer is option 4.***

• The material used in the **Mathura school** was **Spotted Red Sandstone**, which was locally sourced. This is a major distinguishing factor from the **Gandhara school**, which utilized **Grey Schist** or **Blue-grey Schist**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• The feature of **Highly polished sandstone** is a characteristic of **Mauryan Art** (e.g., **Ashokan Pillars**), not the **Mathura school**. The **Mathura** artists focused more on **voluptuousness** and **anatomical details** rather than a mirror-like polish. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• The **Mathura school** was purely **Indian** in its inspiration and execution. In contrast, the **Gandhara school** exhibited **Heavy Greek influence** (Hellenistic style), often referred to as **Greco-Buddhist art**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Geographical Location**: The school was centered around **Mathura** in **Uttar Pradesh**, which served as a major junction for trade and culture during the **Kushana Empire**.

• **Patronage**: The development of this school was heavily supported by the **Kushana rulers**, most notably **King Kanishka**, who was a great patron of **Buddhism** and the arts.

• **Artistic Characteristics**: Sculptures from this school are known for their **fleshy bodies**, **smiling expressions**, and **transparent drapery**. The **Buddha** is often depicted with a **shaved head** or a **protuberance** (Ushnisha) and is frequently shown in the **Abhaya Mudra** (gesture of fearlessness).

• **Secular Art**: Beyond religious icons, the school produced **secular sculptures**, including portraits of kings. A famous example is the **headless statue of Kanishka**, which showcases the **Central Asian** dress style including long tunics and heavy boots.

• **Evolution of Buddha**: In the early stages, **Buddha** was represented through symbols like the **Dharmachakra** or **Bodhi tree**, but the **Mathura school** played a pivotal role in transitioning these into **full-scale human idols**.

**Important Points__**

• **Religious Synthesis**: The **Mathura school** is unique because it simultaneously catered to **Buddhism**, **Jainism**, and **Brahmanism** (Hinduism), reflecting the **religious pluralism** of ancient India.

• **Influence on Later Art**: The techniques and iconographic standards established in **Mathura** laid the foundation for the **Gupta school of art** (4th-6th century AD), which is often described as the **Golden Age** of Indian sculpture.

• **Yakshas and Yakshinis**: The school continued the ancient Indian tradition of carving **Yakshas** and **Yakshinis**, which were fertility deities. These figures were carved with **sensuality** and **elaborate jewelry**, representing the **idealized human form**.

• **Comparison with Gandhara**: While **Gandhara** art focused on **realism** and **muscularity** (similar to **Apollo**), **Mathura art** focused on **inner spirituality** and **grace**.
</ul

questions.question: Arundhati Roy won the Booker Prize in which year for her debut novel 'The God of Small Things'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1997**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Arundhati Roy** was awarded the prestigious **Booker Prize** in the **year 1997**.

• The award was conferred for her **debut novel**, **'The God of Small Things'**, which achieved global critical and commercial success.

• She holds the distinction of being the **first Indian citizen** to win this international literary award, bringing significant recognition to **Indian English literature**.

• The novel is set in **Ayemenem**, a village in the **Kottayam district** of **Kerala**, and captures the complex social and political atmosphere of the **1960s**.

• The story focuses on the lives of **fraternal twins**, **Rahel** and **Esthappen**, and explores deep-seated themes of **caste discrimination**, **communism**, and the **'Love Laws'** that dictate social boundaries in **India**.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Arundhati Roy** was born on **November 24, 1961**, in **Shillong**, **Meghalaya**, to a **Syrian Christian** mother and a **Bengali Hindu** father.

• Beyond her literary achievements, she is a prominent **political activist** and **essayist** who has spoken extensively on **human rights**, **environmental justice**, and the impacts of **globalization**.

• Her second major novel, **'The Ministry of Utmost Happiness'**, was published in **2017**, nearly **20 years** after her debut, and was longlisted for the **Man Booker Prize**.

• She won the **National Film Award** for **Best Screenplay** in **1989** for the film **'In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones'**.

• Some of her notable non-fiction works include **'The Algebra of Infinite Justice'**, **'Power Politics'**, and **'War Talk'**, which critique **neo-imperialism** and **state policies**.

**Important Points__**

• The **Booker Prize** was established in **1969** and is one of the world's most famous literary prizes, awarded annually for the best novel written in **English** and published in the **UK** or **Ireland**.

• Other **Indian** or **Indian-origin** authors who have won the prize include **V.S. Naipaul** (**1971**), **Salman Rushdie** (**1981**), **Kiran Desai** (**2006**), and **Aravind Adiga** (**2008**).

• In **1993**, **Salman Rushdie's** **'Midnight's Children'** was awarded the **'Booker of Bookers'** to commemorate the **25th anniversary** of the prize.

• Winning the **Booker Prize** carries a cash reward of **£50,000** and typically leads to a massive increase in international **book sales** and **translation** into multiple **languages**.

• The prize is currently managed by the **Booker Prize Foundation** and is sponsored by **Crankstart**, a charitable foundation.

questions.question: Which year is considered the approximate composition period of the Natya Shastra, the earliest known treatise on Indian music and dance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**200 BCE**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Natya Shastra** is the most ancient and comprehensive treatise on the performing arts, including **dance**, **music**, and **drama**. It is traditionally attributed to the legendary sage **Bharata Muni**.

• The approximate period of its composition is widely accepted by historians and scholars to be between **200 BCE and 200 CE**. The year **200 BCE** represents the beginning of this classical period of compilation. ***Hence, the correct answer is 200 BCE.***

• The text is written in **Sanskrit** and is composed of approximately **6000 poetic verses** (shlokas) spread across **36 chapters**. It provides a detailed framework for everything from stage design to the emotional states of actors.

• It is often referred to as the **Pancham Veda** or the **Fifth Veda**. This designation signifies its importance as a sacred text that was intended to be accessible to all sections of society, unlike the four primary Vedas.

• The other options, such as **1000 BCE**, **500 CE**, and **1500 CE**, are historically inaccurate. **1000 BCE** corresponds to the early **Vedic period**, while **500 CE** and **1500 CE** belong to the **Gupta** and **Medieval** periods respectively, which are much later than the linguistic and cultural context of the **Natya Shastra**.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Rasa Theory**: The **Natya Shastra** is famous for introducing the concept of **Rasa** (aesthetic essence or sentiment). It lists **eight primary Rasas**: **Shringara** (Love), **Hasya** (Mirth), **Karuna** (Compassion), **Raudra** (Anger), **Veera** (Heroism), **Bhayanaka** (Fear), **Bibhatsa** (Disgust), and **Adbhuta** (Wonder).

• **Classification of Music**: The treatise classifies musical instruments into four distinct categories: **Tata Vadya** (stringed instruments), **Avanaddha Vadya** (percussion instruments like **drums**), **Ghana Vadya** (solid instruments like **cymbals**), and **Sushira Vadya** (wind instruments like **flutes**).

• **Dance Elements**: It describes **108 Karanas** (basic dance movements) and various **Mudras** (hand gestures). These elements form the technical foundation for all **Indian Classical Dance** forms such as **Bharatanatyam**, **Odissi**, and **Kathakali**.

• **Theatrical Architecture**: The text provides specific guidelines for the construction of playhouses (**Natyamandapa**), describing three shapes: **Vikrishta** (rectangular), **Chaturasra** (square), and **Tryasra** (triangular).

**Important Points__**

• **Abhinavagupta**: The most influential commentary on the **Natya Shastra** is the **Abhinavabharati**, written by the **Kashmiri** philosopher **Abhinavagupta** in the **10th-11th century CE**. This commentary is essential for modern interpretations of the text.

• **Gandharva Veda**: The musical science described in the **Natya Shastra** is known as **Gandharva**, which is considered an **Upaveda** of the **Sama Veda**. It focuses on the ritualistic and spiritual power of sound.

• **Shrutis and Swaras**: The text establishes the system of **22 Shrutis** (microtones) and the **seven Swaras** (notes: **Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni**), which remain the bedrock of **Hindustani** and **Carnatic** classical music.

• **Tandava and Lasya**: It distinguishes between **Tandava** (the vigorous, masculine dance attributed to **Lord Shiva**) and **Lasya** (the graceful, feminine dance attributed to **Goddess Parvati**).
</ul

questions.question: According to the 2011 Census, which state in India has the highest proportion of its population living in rural areas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bihar**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• According to the **2011 Census**, **Bihar** has the highest proportion of its population living in rural areas among the given options. Approximately **88.71%** of **Bihar's** population resides in rural regions, while only **11.29%** lives in urban areas. *Hence, this option is correct.*

• While **Bihar** is the answer among the choices provided, **Himachal Pradesh** actually holds the record for the highest rural population percentage in **India** at **89.97%**.

• **Uttar Pradesh** has a very high rural population in absolute numbers, but in terms of proportion, it stands at **77.73%**, which is lower than **Bihar**. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*

• **West Bengal** has a rural population proportion of approximately **68.13%**, with a significant portion of the state being urbanized around the **Kolkata** metropolitan area. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*

• **Goa** is one of the most urbanized states in **India**, with only **37.83%** of its population living in rural areas and **62.17%** living in urban centers. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **2011 Census** revealed that the total **Rural Population** of **India** was **83.3 crore**, accounting for **68.84%** of the total population.

• The **Urban Population** of **India** stood at **37.7 crore**, which is **31.16%** of the total population. This marked a significant increase in urbanization compared to the **2001 Census**.

• **Goa** is the most urbanized state in **India** with **62.17%** urban population, followed by **Mizoram** at **52.1%** and **Tamil Nadu** at **48.4%**.

• **Kerala** and **Maharashtra** also show high levels of urbanization at **47.7%** and **45.2%** respectively.

• Among **Union Territories**, **Delhi** is the most urbanized with **97.5%** of its population living in urban areas, followed by **Chandigarh** at **97.25%**.

**Important Points__**

• In terms of absolute numbers, **Uttar Pradesh** has the largest rural population in **India** with **15.5 crore** people living in villages.

• **Maharashtra** has the highest absolute urban population in the country, with **5.08 crore** people residing in cities and towns.

• The **2011 Census** was the **15th National Census** of **India** since **1872** and the **7th** census after Independence.

• The **Census Commissioner** of **India** during the **2011 Census** was **C. Chandramouli**, and the official motto was **'Our Census, Our Future'**.

• The data is collected by the **Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner**, which falls under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**, Government of **India**.
</ul

questions.question: Which city hosted the first Asian Games in 1951?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**New Delhi**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **First Asian Games**, officially known as the **First Asiad**, were held in **New Delhi**, **India**, in **1951**. This multi-sport event took place from **March 4** to **March 11, 1951**, making **New Delhi** the inaugural host city.

• The games were officially opened by the first **President of India**, **Dr. Rajendra Prasad**, at the **Irwin Stadium**, which was later renamed the **Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium**.

• A total of **11 National Olympic Committees (NOCs)** participated in the first edition, including **Afghanistan**, **Burma**, **Ceylon**, **India**, **Indonesia**, **Iran**, **Japan**, **Nepal**, **Philippines**, **Singapore**, and **Thailand**.

• **Japan** topped the medal table with a total of **60 medals** (including **24 gold**), while the host nation, **India**, finished in **second place** with **51 medals** (including **15 gold**).

• The other options provided are incorrect for the first edition: **Tokyo** hosted the **3rd Asian Games** in **1958**, **Jakarta** hosted the **4th edition** in **1962**, and **Bangkok** hosted its first games in **1966**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Guru Dutt Sondhi**: He is recognized as the **father of the Asian Games**. As an Indian sports administrator and member of the **International Olympic Committee (IOC)**, he proposed the concept of the **Asian Games** to foster friendship and solidarity among Asian nations after **World War II**.

• **Governing Body**: The first games were organized by the **Asian Games Federation (AGF)**. However, since **1982**, the games have been regulated by the **Olympic Council of Asia (OCA)**, which is recognized by the **International Olympic Committee**.

• **Frequency and Scale**: The **Asian Games** are held every **four years** and are considered the **second-largest multi-sport event** in the world, following the **Olympic Games**.

• **India as Host**: **India** has hosted the **Asian Games** twice. After the inaugural **1951** edition, **New Delhi** again hosted the **9th Asian Games** in **1982**, which saw the introduction of the first official mascot, **Appu**, an elephant.

• **Bangkok's Hosting Record**: **Bangkok**, **Thailand**, holds the record for hosting the **Asian Games** the most number of times, having served as the host city in **1966**, **1970**, **1978**, and **1998**.

**Important Points__**

• **Sports and Disciplines**: The **1951 Asian Games** featured **6 sports**: **Athletics**, **Aquatics** (Swimming, Diving, and Water Polo), **Basketball**, **Cycling** (Road and Track), **Football**, and **Weightlifting**. A total of **489 athletes** competed in **57 events**.

• **Official Motto**: The motto for the first games was **'Play the Game, in the Spirit of the Game'**, a phrase coined by the first **Prime Minister of India**, **Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru**. The official permanent motto of the **OCA** is **'Ever Onward'**.

• **Torch Relay**: The tradition of the **torch relay** for the **Asian Games** began at the **Red Fort** in **New Delhi** during the **1951** edition, where the flame was lit by the sun's rays using a parabolic mirror.

• **Notable Achievements**: Indian sprinter **Lavy Pinto** became the first **Indian** to win a **gold medal** in the **Asian Games**, securing victories in both the **100-meter** and **200-meter** sprints in **1951**.

• **Recent and Future Editions**: The **19th Asian Games** were held in **Hangzhou**, **China**, in **2023** (postponed from **2022**). The **20th edition** is scheduled to be held in **Aichi-Nagoya**, **Japan**, in **2026**.
</ul

questions.question: Who founded Harijan Sangh and contended that the Shastras did not approve untouchability; and if they did, they should be disregarded?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahatma Gandhi**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Mahatma Gandhi** founded the **Harijan Sevak Sangh** on **30 September 1932**. This organization was established to eradicate **untouchability** in India and uplift the depressed classes. ***Hence, the statement about the founder is correct.***

• Gandhi strongly contended that the **Shastras** (ancient Hindu scriptures) did not provide any religious sanction for the practice of **untouchability**. He viewed it as a **social evil** that had crept into **Hinduism** over time.

• He famously argued that if any **scripture** were found to support **untouchability**, it should be **disregarded** as it would be contrary to the fundamental principles of **Truth** and **Non-violence** (Ahimsa).

• **Rabindranath Tagore** was a world-renowned poet and philosopher who founded **Visva-Bharati University** in **1921**. While he supported social reforms, he was not the founder of the **Harijan Sevak Sangh**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

• **Gopal Krishna Gokhale** was a moderate political leader and the founder of the **Servants of India Society** in **1905**. He served as a mentor to Gandhi but passed away in **1915**, long before the **Harijan Sangh** was formed. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

• **Jyotiba Phule** was a pioneering social reformer from **Maharashtra** who founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj** in **1873**. Although he was a champion for the rights of the lower castes, he was not associated with the **Harijan Sevak Sangh** founded in the **20th century**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Harijan Sevak Sangh**: Originally named the **All India Anti-Untouchability League**, it was later renamed by Gandhi. The headquarters of the organization is located at **Kingsway Camp** in **Delhi**.

• **Leadership**: The first president of the **Harijan Sevak Sangh** was the prominent industrialist **Ghanshyam Das Birla**, and the first secretary was **Amritlal Thakkar**, popularly known as **Thakkar Bapa**.

• **Satyashodhak Samaj**: Founded by **Jyotiba Phule** in **Pune**, this society aimed to liberate the **Shudra** and **Untouchable** castes from exploitation by upper castes. Phule also wrote the famous book **Gulamgiri** in **1873**.

• **Servants of India Society**: Established by **Gokhale** in **Pune**, its objective was to train **national missionaries** for the service of India and to promote the true interests of the Indian people through constitutional means.

• **Visva-Bharati**: Located in **Santiniketan**, **West Bengal**, it was declared a **Central University** and an institution of national importance in **1951**. **Tagore** envisioned it as a place where the world makes a home in a single nest.

**Important Points__**

• **Poona Pact (1932)**: The **Harijan Sevak Sangh** was a direct outcome of the **Poona Pact** signed between **Mahatma Gandhi** and **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**. This pact was reached after Gandhi's fast in **Yerwada Jail** against the **Communal Award** of **Ramsay MacDonald**.

• **Harijan Journal**: To spread his message against **untouchability**, Gandhi started a weekly journal named **Harijan** in **1933**. He also published **Harijan Bandu** in **Gujarati** and **Harijan Sevak** in **Hindi**.

• **Harijan Tour**: Between **November 1933** and **July 1934**, Gandhi undertook a **nationwide tour** known as the **Harijan Tour**, covering about **20,000 kilometers** to collect funds (**Harijan Fund**) and mobilize public opinion against the practice of **untouchability**.
</ul

questions.question: Why did Mahatma Gandhi call for a campaign against the Rowlatt Act?

options.text: During the non-cooperation movement, thousands of Indians were kept in jail
British censorship of press and permitted detention without trial
Hundreds of people were killed in the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
Sir Sidney Rowlatt was a Britisher

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**British censorship of press and permitted detention without trial**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Rowlatt Act**, officially known as the **Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919**, was a legislative act passed by the **Imperial Legislative Council** in **Delhi** on **18th March 1919**.
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi** called for a nationwide campaign against this act because it authorized the **British Government** to imprison people suspected of terrorism for up to **two years** without any trial. This violated the basic principle of **civil liberty** and judicial fairness. ***Hence, the statement regarding detention without trial is correct.***
 
• The act also provided for the **censorship of the press**, allowing the colonial administration to control and suppress the flow of information and nationalist propaganda. ***Hence, the statement regarding censorship of the press is correct.***
 
• The **Non-cooperation movement** (1920-22) happened after the Rowlatt Satyagraha; therefore, the jailing of Indians during that movement was not the reason for Gandhi's initial call against the Rowlatt Act. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• While the **Jallianwala Bagh massacre** (13th April 1919) was a direct consequence of the protests against the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of leaders like **Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew** and **Dr. Satyapal**, it was not the reason why Gandhi initially called for the campaign. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• Although **Sir Sidney Rowlatt** was indeed a **British judge** who headed the committee, his nationality was not the primary reason for the protest; rather, it was the draconian nature of the laws he recommended. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Rowlatt Committee:** The act was based on the report of the **Sedition Committee** of **1918**, chaired by **Sir Sidney Rowlatt**. The committee was tasked with investigating the **revolutionary conspiracies** of the Indian nationalist movement and suggesting measures to curb them.
 
• **The Black Act:** Gandhi and other Indian leaders referred to the Rowlatt Act as the **Black Act**. The popular slogan associated with the protest was **No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal**, meaning there was no right to argument, no right to a lawyer, and no right to appeal against the detention.
 
• **Rowlatt Satyagraha:** Gandhi organized the **Satyagraha Sabha** in **Bombay** to direct the movement. He called for a nationwide **hartal** (strike) on **6th April 1919**, which was observed as a day of **humiliation and prayer** and a protest against the unjust law.
 
• **Resignations:** In protest against the passing of the act, prominent Indian members of the **Imperial Legislative Council**, including **Madan Mohan Malaviya**, **Mazhar-ul-Haq**, and **Mohammed Ali Jinnah**, resigned from their seats.
 
• **Impact on National Movement:** The Rowlatt Satyagraha was the first **all-India struggle** against the British government, although it was largely restricted to cities. It marked the transition of the Indian national movement from an elite-driven struggle to a **mass-based movement** under the leadership of **Mahatma Gandhi**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Punjab Unrest:** The protests were particularly intense in **Punjab**, especially in **Amritsar** and **Lahore**. The government responded with **martial law**, which eventually culminated in the **Jallianwala Bagh Massacre** on **13th April 1919**, where **General Dyer** ordered troops to fire on a peaceful gathering.
 
• **Withdrawal of Satyagraha:** Seeing the violence that erupted following the massacre and the government's brutal repression, **Mahatma Gandhi** withdrew the **Rowlatt Satyagraha** on **18th April 1919**, calling it a **Himalayan Blunder** because the people were not yet fully trained in the methods of **non-violence**.
 
• **Legislative Context:** The act was passed despite the **unanimous opposition** of every single Indian member of the council, highlighting the **autocratic nature** of British rule in India during that period.

questions.question: Which four countries make up the Quad?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**USA, Japan, India, Australia**__.
